claims.text: Atomic-radius mismatch produces variations in interatomic separations and static local lattice distortion in solid-solution alloys.
Electronegativity differences among constituent elements contribute to local chemical or chemical-bond fluctuations.
The combined degree of static lattice distortion and local chemical fluctuation governs whether equimolar multi-metal nanoparticles retain a single-phase solid solution from 473 K to 1923 K.
Element substitution based on atomic-radius and electronegativity disparities can systematically vary local lattice distortion while retaining equimolarity.
Atomic-size mismatch and chemical fluctuation jointly generate local lattice distortions.
Static interatomic-length disorder and temperature-induced dynamic distortion can be represented through a unified effective-temperature scaling.
Increasing lattice distortion elevates an effective temperature that raises the energetic barrier to phase separation or chemical ordering.
The raised barrier suppresses detrimental atomic rearrangements and thereby preserves a single-phase solid solution over a broad temperature range.
Nanoparticles with greater lattice distortion will retain a single-phase structure up to 1923 K better than lower-distortion controls.
Nanoparticles with greater lattice distortion will maintain more stable catalytic properties across 473–1923 K.
Nanoparticles with greater lattice distortion will maintain more stable thermoelectric properties across 473–1923 K.
Low-distortion nanoparticles will undergo phase segregation or ordering at lower temperatures than high-distortion nanoparticles.
The original nanoparticles have moderate inherent lattice distortion that provides some stability at moderate temperatures.
Particle-size effects, surface oxidation, or non-equilibrium behavior can dominate the intrinsic structural response and limit the prediction.
Nanoscale surface-to-volume ratios and defect densities may modify the proposed distortion-based stabilization mechanism relative to bulk materials.
